name: Rafael Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. Walk me through a normal shift on the lines.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We start at the electricity company yard, check the truck, then take whatever the dispatch board hands us. My apprenticeship taught me to slow down at the pole: isolate the line, test it, then let the crew climb. I am forty-three and still like restoring a street after a storm, though the callout rota can swallow a family dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the yard I would say the AI fuss has not changed a wet pole or a broken crossarm. A quicker form would be welcome, but I would keep the crew’s check at the site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I sometimes use an AI tool to tidy a note, and I still reread every line. My wage is high for this work and our savings cover over six months, so a small software change does not threaten the mortgage. A polished AI note can still send the next line crew to the wrong pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would carry on taking the rota and checking work orders against the address at the pole. In the first year I would show one apprentice how I verify a generated note against the actual repair, then keep our current household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. My partner and I already have to juggle two school timetables, and this picture adds little to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where could a tidy note still cause trouble?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wrong pole number can send the next crew to the wrong street. I would compare the generated note with the meter number and the crew’s handwritten record before filing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say we can keep the mortgage payment and school costs as planned. We have a cushion and I do not expect line shifts to disappear in this picture.

say: **Small** AI tools can tidy forms, but the crew still tests and repairs each power line.
I would **keep** site checks even when a generated work note looks polished.
think: Our **higher** lineworker pay and savings make minor software changes manageable alongside the mortgage.
An **AI** generated note can still send a crew to the wrong pole if nobody checks it.
do: **Continue** the callout rota and verify work orders against pole addresses.
**Show** an apprentice how to compare a generated note with a real repair record.
feel: **Calm** about lineworker income, with ordinary family scheduling still demanding attention.
S0.quote: A polished AI note can still send the next line crew to the wrong pole.
fieldNote: He **already** uses AI occasionally but keeps the site and handwritten record as the source of truth.
**Six** months of savings and higher wages protect the mortgage from a minor form change.

steps.text: Continue callout rota and verify work orders at each pole
Show apprentice how to verify AI generated repair notes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that smarter dispatch might save miles, provided the crew can correct a bad route. I would want our union to see the travel and repair times before any new productivity target is set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning jobs could thin out while our field work stays busy. I am less worried about a robot taking my place soon than about a computer deciding a storm repair should take half an hour. A computer may save us ten minutes of driving and then demand thirty minutes less for the repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would test the new route suggestions on our regular callouts and log where they send us down a closed road. In the first year I would take those records to our union work group and ask for a joint review of the timing targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, because bad targets turn a useful tool into a fight at the end of the shift. I could handle the tool itself if people who use it can report mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Give me one route error you would write down.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If dispatch sends us over a bridge closed to heavy trucks, I would mark the detour, extra minutes and the callout number. That shows the problem without asking anyone to take my word for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who needs to be in that joint review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A dispatcher, a crew leader and a union representative should look at the same calls. I would also want the person setting the targets to explain how travel time is counted.

say: **Smarter** dispatch may cut travel, provided crews can correct wrong routes before targets are set.
I would **ask** the union to review travel and repair times with management.
think: **Office** planning work may shrink before physical line repairs do.
My **immediate** risk is a computer assigning unrealistic storm repair times, rather than replacing my hands.
do: **Test** suggested routes on callouts and log detours with callout numbers.
**Take** travel records to the union work group for a joint timing review.
feel: **Uneasy** about unfair targets but willing to test a useful routing tool.
S1.quote: A computer may save us ten minutes of driving and then demand thirty minutes less for the repair.
fieldNote: He is **willing** to trial proven tools while insisting that workers see the data behind targets.
His **worry** is compressed repair time, not immediate replacement on physical line work.

steps.text: Test dispatch route suggestions and log detours on callouts
Take route records to union work group for joint review

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that full thinking AI by 2028 could change dispatch and fault plans quickly, with capable robots around 2031. We need paid practice on any robot before it goes near a live line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first change may reach the people who send us out, then the machines can reach the climb three years later. My savings buy time, but losing our higher wage would change what our two children can do, and the mortgage is still there. Our savings can carry the mortgage for a while; they cannot carry two children through a vanished lineworker wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request a paid place on the company’s robot trial crew this year, and ask our union to demand a worker stop button and clear responsibility for errors. In the first year after 2028 I would save an extra hundred from each monthly pay packet and compare nearby electricity company vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I can put my hands to a plan. The speed worries me more than the idea of learning a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the trial crew turned you down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union representative when another paid trial opens, then watch a demonstration without signing off the equipment. I would not leave a well-paid line shift for an unpaid promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why look at other companies if the robot can do the same job there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to know which nearby companies offer actual retraining and which only offer a slogan. Plenty of similar jobs are close by, but I would move only for a real paid role.

say: **Full** thinking AI could alter dispatch by 2028; capable line robots around 2031 require paid crew practice.
I would **ask** the union for a stop button and clear responsibility during trials.
think: **Savings** give me time, but losing higher wages would affect children and mortgage.
**Nearby** employers may offer different training terms even if the technology reaches them too.
do: **Request** a paid place on the electricity company robot trial crew.
**Ask** the union for worker stop controls and written fault responsibility.
**Save** one hundred more per month and compare nearby lineworker vacancies after 2028.
feel: **Anxious** about the short gap, yet able to pursue paid practice and a savings plan.
S2.quote: Our savings can carry the mortgage for a while; they cannot carry two children through a vanished lineworker wage.
fieldNote: He **connects** the fast scenario to children’s options rather than only his own career.
His **job** search is a comparison of paid offers, while trial participation depends on pay.

steps.text: Request paid place on company robot trial crew
Ask union for robot stop controls and written fault responsibility
Save one hundred extra monthly from pay after 2028
Compare paid lineworker vacancies at nearby electricity companies after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say 2031 gives us time to learn which robot trials work before hands-on machines arrive around 2034. The union and company should publish the failures as well as the clean demonstrations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be suited to testing equipment because I know the ordinary faults, not just the spectacular ones. Still, a trial post has to pay enough to cover the mortgage; a title alone does nothing for our family. A robot test that only shows the clean days tells a lineworker almost nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask the company training office for the robot inspection course timetable and pay scale. If a paid course and a trial technician position are offered, I would enroll before 2031 and apply for the role in the first year after full thinking AI arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but the extra years let me look at actual results. I would rather learn after other crews have found the faults than be a brave face at a launch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What result would persuade you the course is worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to see a machine stop safely when a pole is damaged or the weather turns. I would also ask whether the course certificate counts for a paid trial technician vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the callout rota and ask again when paid training opens. We have savings, but paying the mortgage while I train for free is a needless gamble.

say: A **few** years permit open reporting of failed line robot trials before hands-on deployment around 2034.
I would **support** a paid trial technician path if field evidence and pay are sound.
think: **Ordinary** fault experience might help test equipment, subject to mortgage-covering pay.
I would **learn** from other crews’ trials before taking a role myself.
do: **Request** robot inspection course dates, pay scale and certificate value this year.
**Enroll** before 2031 if the company offers a paid course tied to vacancies.
**Apply** for a paid trial technician role after 2031 if the salary covers the mortgage.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to examine results over several years before making a job move.
S3.quote: A robot test that only shows the clean days tells a lineworker almost nothing.
fieldNote: He could **change** roles through an evidence based trial path, with explicit pay and certificate conditions.
**Course** enquiry alone is not counted as retraining; enrollment depends on a paid offer.

steps.text: Enroll in paid robot inspection course before 2031 if offered
Apply for trial technician role after 2031 if pay covers mortgage
Keep line callouts if paid training or suitable role is unavailable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our crew that ten years is long enough to put proper robot testing into the apprenticeship program. If hands-on machines arrive around 2039, the people using them should have helped write the checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At fifty-three when thinking AI arrives, I may want fewer storm nights, though I cannot know what my health or the mortgage balance will be. A paid trainer role might fit if the children are more independent and the hours are real. The robot manual belongs beside the damaged pole, where an apprentice can prove it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask the apprenticeship coordinator whether experienced lineworkers can qualify as paid practical trainers. If that route exists, I would complete the required assessor course during the next two years and apply for a trainer opening when one is posted, while keeping my callout shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm about my own earnings with that much time. I like a plan where the crew helps shape the machines instead of waiting for instructions from a sales room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach that a robot manual misses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would teach apprentices how a damaged crossarm changes the safe approach, and then let them question the robot’s proposed route. A manual should be checked against the pole in front of you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you call the trainer post early retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would still be working and earning a wage. If the hours help me see my children more, that is a job change, not leaving work.

say: A **decade** allows crews to add robot checks to lineworker apprenticeships before hands-on machines arrive around 2039.
**People** using the machines should help write field checks.
think: A **paid** trainer role could reduce storm nights if family needs and mortgage allow.
**Future** health and mortgage balance are unknown, so I would not promise myself a trainer post today.
do: **Ask** apprenticeship coordinator about paid practical trainer qualifications this year.
**Complete** assessor course within two years if the trainer route exists.
**Apply** for a paid trainer opening while keeping callout shifts until an offer arrives.
feel: **Calm** about having time to shape a future role and maintain earnings.
S4.quote: The robot manual belongs beside the damaged pole, where an apprentice can prove it wrong.
fieldNote: He **sees** an eventual training role as continued paid work, not retirement.
A **ten-year** runway lets him plan around storm nights without assuming future debt or health.

steps.text: Complete assessor course within two years if paid trainer route exists
Apply for paid practical trainer opening when posted
Keep callout shifts until a suitable trainer offer arrives

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the thinking systems could remake dispatch before crews have learned to challenge them, and robots follow around 2031. Paid trial places, a worker stop control, and honest reports on failed tests would help. I can learn a tool; I cannot explain a hidden mistake to a family whose lights went out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the apprentices when a robot takes the easiest climbs. They still need real faults to learn from, or the next generation of trainers will only know the manual. I would like the company and union to plan that together.

headlineQuote: I can learn a tool; I cannot explain a hidden mistake to a family whose lights went out.
portrait: **Rafael** is an experienced forty-three-year-old electricity company lineworker who checks pole addresses, isolation steps and repair notes against field evidence.
His **higher** wage and more than six months of savings support a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
He **sometimes** uses AI for notes and will test routing or robots when workers can record errors and challenge targets.
**Fast** AGI makes him save from pay and compare jobs; longer timelines open paid technician or trainer paths if terms work.
biggestWorry: **Fast** AGI by 2028 could change dispatch before crews can challenge errors, with capable line robots following around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** robot trials, worker stop controls, and honest reports of failed tests would let crews learn safely.
